title: Finishing Milk Run for Small Machine Shops
one_liner: A scheduled truck route and capacity-slot exchange that pools small lots from many shops into full tank loads and racks at platers, anodizers, heat treaters and powder coaters.
customer: Job shops and small OEM plants (5-150 employees) that machine or fabricate parts but outsource plating, anodize, passivation, heat treat, e-coat or powder coat. The buyer is the shop owner or plant manager. The second customer is the finisher, who gets fuller tanks and lines.
problem: Everyone talks about a shortage of machinists, but the real reshoring bottleneck is finishing. Parts wait 9-15 days for a truck and for enough volume to fill a tank or rack. Finishers apply minimum-charge lots that punish small runs. Shops drive parts themselves or pay LTL rates of $150-$300 per pallet, and a batch's lead time is mostly waiting, not processing. The 2026 Reshoring Initiative data show finishing capacity as part of the bottleneck, and permits make new capacity slow and rare.
solution: Run daily box-truck routes around a dense corridor (Akron-Canton-Cleveland-Youngstown) with QR-coded totes and text-message status. Pre-buy weekly capacity slots at 8-12 vetted finishers, pool many shops' small lots into shared racks, and guarantee 3-5 day door-to-door turnaround. Route data and slot utilisation decide which finisher gets which parts. Expand to a second corridor (Columbus-Dayton-Cincinnati) once route density works.
why_now: Reshoring is adding machined and fabricated volume in the US while environmental permits have made new plating, anodize and coating lines almost impossible to build. Existing finishers are running full but inefficiently. Lightweight route and tote software plus cheap dispatch tools remove the reason this stayed a hand-arranged, phone-call business.
revenue_model: $55-$95 per stop or tote pickup, an 8-12% margin on capacity-slot resale, and a $299/month booking and tracking subscription. Roughly 40 active shops on one corridor gets to $1M ARR. Later, purchase or co-develop a permitted finishing line inside a 'factory condo'.
non_obvious_insight: An anodize or zinc cycle takes hours. Most of the lead time is a batch waiting for a truck and waiting for enough peers to fill a rack. That is a logistics-and-pooling problem hiding inside what everyone treats as a process-capacity problem, and it is solvable without building a single tank.
first_30_days: Lease one box truck or contract a local courier per stop. Interview 15 shops and 4 finishers. Launch one route on Tuesdays and Thursdays with 8 pilot shops at $65 per stop. Get two finishers to guarantee 48-hour processing for pooled lots in exchange for weekly committed volume. Track everything in Airtable with printed QR tags and text updates, and publish on-time-in-full data after 6 weeks.

title: Drone-Ready Rx Lockers as Adherence Infrastructure
one_liner: A lockable, temperature-buffered, authenticated receiving station at a senior's home that accepts drone or courier drops and quietly reports whether the medication was retrieved.
customer: Medicare Advantage plans and pharmacy chains, paying per active station plus per delivery. Independent-living communities are the pilot channel.
problem: Drone delivery is scaling (Wing/Walmart 270+ sites by 2027, Lowe's launch on Sep 28, 2026), but a 78-year-old cannot reliably receive a 2.5 lb drop. Bending, theft, weather and controlled-substance rules get in the way. Plans lose Star Ratings money on medication non-adherence, and solo agers have no daily check-in.
solution: A roughly $120 bill-of-materials box (porch, balcony or window mounted) with recipient authentication, insulation and a retrieval sensor. Start with human courier deliveries into the same locker, and add drone-network integration as it opens. A missed-retrieval alert goes to the pharmacy, then the family.
why_now: Retail drone networks are now big enough to need a receiving standard. Part D adherence measures are triple-weighted in Star Ratings. Medicare Advantage benefit cuts (OTC benefits from 9.6% to 2.4% of plans) push plans to look for outcome-linked spend.
revenue_model: $8-15 per month per station from plans or pharmacies, plus a per-retrieval fee to drone operators or pharmacies. Optional hardware financing.
non_obvious_insight: The delivery event is the cheapest, least creepy daily proof-of-life signal, and no camera or wearable is needed. The receiving end, not the flight, is the missing piece of senior drone delivery.
first_30_days: Build 20 units. Place them in two independent-living communities where the operator controls the landing zone. Sign an independent pharmacy chain for human-courier deliveries. Bring adherence and retrieval data to one MA plan's pharmacy team.

title: Pet Sitters as Home-Energy Field Workforce
one_liner: A trained, insured network of pet sitters and dog walkers who already hold house keys and midday access, performing unlicensed home-energy tasks that stall electrification programs.
customer: VPP and DR aggregators, utility weatherization and heat pump programs, and home-battery/heat-pump installers that pay per completed visit ($40-90). Homeowners see it as free or discounted enrollment.
problem: Electricians are scarce (about 81,000 openings a year) and data centers pay 25-30% premiums, so home electrification loses labor. But many program stalls are not licensed work: 'customer must be home' no-shows, devices offline, thermostat and smart-plug swaps, filter changes, weatherstripping, photos for interconnection paperwork, and plug-in solar setup. Each one is a truck roll priced like an electrician's.
solution: Recruit and background-check pet sitters and walkers, insure them, and train them on about a dozen no-license tasks with guided QR workflows. Schedule tasks alongside pet visits, with the owner's explicit opt-in and strict limits (plug-in and low-voltage only, no panel work). Route orders from utilities, VPP operators and installers, and include placement of pet-zone sensors where relevant.
why_now: Data-center wage arbitrage is draining electricians (one report shows $20 to $35 an hour), 25C/25D subsidies ended so programs are cutting cost per home, and at least nine states have signed plug-in solar laws (around 1.2 kW, UL 3700 exists), which makes non-electrician installs legal and needed.
revenue_model: Per-visit fee billed to the program ($40-90) with 25-35% margin after sitter pay, training and certification fees, and a subscription for large programs that need a managed scheduling and QA layer.
non_obvious_insight: The energy transition's shortage is not just electricians. A large slice of tasks need access and trust rather than a license, and pet sitters uniquely hold both, visit on a schedule, and are a labor pool data centers cannot poach.
first_30_days: Pick one metro where a local sitter collective or Rover/Wag-heavy sitter community exists. Recruit and train 20 sitters on 5 tasks (thermostat, smart plug, offline-device reconnect, filter swap, plug-in solar setup). Sell a pilot at $60/visit to one co-op or heat-pump installer needing post-install commissioning and connectivity fixes. Confirm liability coverage before the first visit.

title: Sponsor-a-Lifeline Satellite Messaging for Missionaries
one_liner: A church-sponsored satellite messaging line plus supporter-update relay for missionaries, Bible translators and mission-aviation crews in no-coverage areas, sold to mission agencies as duty of care.
customer: Mission agencies with 50-2,000 field workers and the sending churches that sponsor individual workers.
problem: Field workers live outside coverage and agencies carry duty of care using a patchwork of individual satellite communicators. Missionaries also fund themselves through supporter updates, which stall when connectivity is bad. Churches want a tangible way to care for their people, yet direct-to-cell carriers still do not know how to price or differentiate satellite service.
solution: A neutral bundle: direct-to-cell or handheld messaging across whichever networks work (Iridium NTN, Starlink direct-to-cell, others) plus an agency dashboard with check-in cadence, geofenced security alerts and evacuation triggers. Short satellite texts are compiled into a 'prayer letter' for supporters, and a sponsor page (for example 'Sponsor Anna's lifeline at $18 per month') keeps privacy controls.
why_now: Satellite-to-phone partnerships are multiplying but 'key questions remain unresolved' on pricing and value (Satellite Today, Sept 2026). Iridium NTN Direct is expected later in 2026, and Starlink ARPU falling from $81 to $66 signals cheaper plans. Carriers and resellers need verticals with a willing payer.
revenue_model: $15-25 per field worker per month paid by the agency or sponsors, a $150-200 hardware and setup margin, and enterprise duty-of-care dashboard tiers.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the sending church or agency, not the traveler, and the value of connectivity is fundraising continuity as much as SOS. A 'sponsor a lifeline' framing turns safety hardware into recurring giving.
first_30_days: Approach 5 small and mid-sized agencies through a mission-agency association. Offer 20-seat pilots at $150 setup plus $18 per month per seat. Write prayer-letter templates and test the sponsor page with two sending churches.

title: Family Bank: Bank of Mom and Dad, Papered
one_liner: A family office's real job is governance and records, not investing; for $20/mo, give ordinary parents and adult children a promissory-note, autopay and sibling-fairness ledger for the money that already flows between them.
customer: Parents aged 55-75 who lend or give money to adult children (down-payment help, car, tuition, debt payoff, business start), sold as a pair with the adult child (28-45). Elder-law attorneys, mortgage brokers and credit unions are referral channels.
problem: Family lending is handshake-based. Zero-interest loans over $10k invite imputed-interest questions. Gifts above the $19,000 annual exclusion (2026) need Form 709 filings. Medicaid's 60-month look-back treats gifts and forgiven loans as transfers. Mortgage lenders want documented gift letters. Siblings fight at inheritance over who got what because nobody kept records. NAR's 2025 profile shows the median first-time buyer is 40 and 22% received a gift or loan from relatives or friends.
solution: A guided flow decides gift vs loan and generates a note at or above the AFR (August 2026: 4.10% short, 4.35% mid, 4.92% long). ACH autopay collects and pays, and both sides get annual interest statements. A December 'forgiveness engine' forgives up to the exclusion with proper letters. A sibling ledger records every advancement so estates can equalize. Flags fire for Form 709 and Medicaid look-back exposure, and there is a mortgage-ready gift-letter generator plus one-click export to the family's estate attorney. Attorney review is an add-on.
why_now: Median first-time buyer age hit 40 (a record), housing costs push more family help, and long-term-care costs make the Medicaid look-back a live worry for boomer parents. Instant-payment and bank-linking rails make autopay cheap. The 2026 federal estate exemption is $15M, so for most families the value is peace and records, not tax planning.
revenue_model: $20/mo per family (up to 3 active loans); $49 document packs for the free-to-paid funnel; $149 attorney review add-on with referral fees; optional servicing fee; later, a pooled family reserve product.
non_obvious_insight: The killer feature is not the loan, it is the sibling ledger. Most family money fights are about unequal treatment nobody can prove, and family offices solve this with an advancement ledger that ordinary families never get. The loan-vs-gift label is also the pivot point for tax and Medicaid consequences, so classification is the paid moment.
first_30_days: Ship a free AFR calculator and note generator aimed at 'family loan agreement' searches, and sell $49 document packs. Convert 5% to the $20/mo servicing tier. Line up 3 elder-law attorneys who receive leads and review notes. Target 50 paying families.

title: Real-Factory Credentials From Customs Shipping Records
one_liner: Turn public US import records into supplier-owned reputation credentials and audit-ready reasonable-care dossiers that prove a factory is a real manufacturer.
customer: Small and mid-size US importers of record (Amazon and Shopify brands, furniture, hardware and apparel distributors) re-sourcing to Vietnam, India, Mexico and Turkey. Customs brokers are a channel, and factories are the second payer.
problem: The importer of record is investigated first, and liability turns on whether it exercised reasonable care about the supplier's origin claims. In August 2026 the White House published a report on transshipment, a 40% penalty tariff applies, and CBP has expanded inspections of shipments from Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Mexico. Small importers cannot tell a real factory from a trading company or a re-labeller, and sourcing agents' claims are unverifiable.
solution: Supplier Proof. Build a profile per factory from three or more years of US import records (shipper and consignee names, volumes, product codes, ports, cadence) plus corporate registry and location data, flag anomalies such as volume beyond plausible capacity, mismatched product codes or shell-company addresses, and add optional local inspector visits. Factories claim and verify their profile and can consent to name repeat buyers as references. The output is a dossier the importer can hand to a broker or to CBP.
why_now: Tariff enforcement moved in 2025-26 from headline rates to origin verification, and the August 2026 transshipment report has put importer liability on every compliance officer's desk. Sourcing shifts away from China are happening now, so millions of dollars of orders are going to unfamiliar factories.
revenue_model: Importer subscriptions of $149-499 per month, $150-400 per dossier, inspector visits passed through at a margin, and $600-1,200 per year from factories for a verified credential once importers demand it.
non_obvious_insight: Import records are the only unforgeable cross-border reputation ledger for factories, but they are sold as raw rows to analysts. Repackaged as supplier-owned credentials with a reasonable-care wrapper, a data product becomes a compliance product with a real budget line: avoiding a 40% penalty.
first_30_days: Buy 12 months of import records for two categories (for example furniture and hardware from Vietnam and India). Auto-build about 1,000 factory profiles and hand-audit 20. Send 200 emails to sourcing managers and customs brokers. Sell the first 10 dossiers at $250 each and use them to refine the scoring.

title: Made-in-USA Proof Files for Relabeling Brands
one_liner: Audit-ready substantiation files and monitoring for brands rushing to claim 'Made in USA' after tariffs.
customer: Consumer and industrial brands with $5M-$300M revenue and retailer private-label teams, buying through general counsel or the ecommerce head.
problem: Tariffs make US-made claims valuable, but an unqualified 'Made in USA' claim needs 'all or virtually all' US content and processing under FTC rules, with civil penalties per violation and state-law class actions on top. Brands switch suppliers on cost and forget the claim. Suppliers cannot document origin per component.
solution: Software plus service that maps each SKU's BOM to component and labor origin, gathers supplier attestations and mill certs, scores the claim, drafts compliant packaging and listing language ('Assembled in USA with global parts', or percent US), monitors marketplace listings and supplier changes, and builds a defense binder.
why_now: A reshoring marketing wave, supplier switching under tariffs, and active enforcement risk. The same BOM data that supports tariff compliance supports the claim.
revenue_model: $3-15k per product-line audit plus $500-2k a month for monitoring. Retailer programs that require proof.
non_obvious_insight: The first legal casualty of the reshoring wave is the label. Brands that reshore partially and market fully carry hidden liability, and a file built once serves both marketing and customs defense. The buyer is legal or marketing, not customs, so this avoids the crowded tariff-software budget.
first_30_days: Scan Amazon 'Made in USA' listings for weak claims using public data. Send a three-page claim risk scorecard to the brands. Sell the first 10 audits at $3k with a partner advertising lawyer signing off.

title: Live-In Caretaker Tenants for Homes in Probate
one_liner: A managed service that places vetted short-term tenants in homes stuck in probate. The rent covers carrying costs, the occupied status keeps the house insured, and the estate gets a caretaker instead of a vacant liability.
customer: Executors and heirs (often out-of-state and aged 50-65), and the probate attorneys, realtors and bank trust officers who advise them. Tenants (traveling nurses, displaced workers, downsizing seniors) pay a reduced rent.
problem: Probate takes months to a year and a half, and the house sits empty. Standard homeowner policies typically restrict coverage after 30-60 days of vacancy, and vacant-property policies cost far more. Break-ins and burst pipes are common, and the executor pays taxes, utilities and insurance. August 2026 was the strongest buyer's market on Redfin's record (58% more sellers than buyers, 44.7% of sales with concessions), so sales take longer. Meanwhile 20% of renter households paid late or missed rent in 2025.
solution: Provide a state-specific rolling license or lease template (executor-authority checked by counsel), tenant vetting, an occupied-dwelling insurance rider through a partner MGA, utilities in the caretaker's name, monthly inspections, an inventory with valuables and documents locked away, and a clean turnover at closing. Tenants pay about 70-85% of market rent. The estate pays a flat management fee that is typically below its avoided vacancy costs. The referral funnel is estate attorneys and probate realtors.
why_now: Rates near 7.5% and record concessions lengthen time-to-sale. The first wave of the wealth transfer is spousal, and hundreds of thousands of homes a year pass through death. Middle-income rent distress is at a series high, and rents are flat nationally, so a discounted, furnished, month-to-month home has a ready tenant pool. AI-armed pro se tenants are a rising risk, which makes well-drafted licenses and vetting a real edge.
revenue_model: About 10% of rent or a flat $250 per month per house, a setup fee, insurance and utility referral commissions, and an upsell into cleanout, staging and listing.
non_obvious_insight: The dead-owner house is the one kind of housing supply that is empty by legal necessity rather than by demand. It stays empty because nobody has authority, insurance or know-how to rent it. Probate delay is a housing-supply constraint disguised as a legal process.
first_30_days: Sign three probate attorneys as partners. Have counsel draft a license for one state. Recruit about 10 tenant candidates through traveling-nurse agencies, colleges and displaced-worker groups. Get an MGA to quote an occupied rider. Pilot three houses in one county.

title: Independent audit desk for city surveillance vendors
one_liner: A fixed-price monthly service that checks whether a city's license-plate-reader and drone vendor is actually following the city's own sharing rules, and hands the council a report it can cite.
customer: City auditors, city attorneys and city managers (plus police oversight boards) in the roughly 50+ cities that cancelled or suspended Flock and the many more that kept ALPR or drone programs under new council conditions. Buyers pay $1.2k-2.5k/month per city from the auditor, city attorney or IT budget, well under the informal-procurement threshold.
problem: Cities cannot verify what the surveillance vendor does with their data. Mountain View's own audit found a statewide-lookup setting active on 29 of 30 cameras since program start, with 250+ outside agencies running about 600,000 searches in 12 months, and the vendor kept no records that would show what was shared. Oxnard's vendor silently re-enabled a nationwide query feature. Evanston found cameras reinstalled after cancellation. Dayton found 7,100+ searches for immigration enforcement that city policy prohibited. Councils now write audit duties into ordinances, but the auditor's office has no tooling.
solution: A vendor-neutral audit service (Flock, Axon, Motorola/Vigilant, drone platforms). The city exports the search and audit logs and sharing-settings screenshots it can already download. The service ingests them and runs a rules engine against the city's adopted policy: searches with no case number or with vague reason codes, out-of-state or federal agencies, immigration-related terms, off-hours spikes, and diffs of the network-sharing settings month to month to catch silent config changes. Output is a council-ready quarterly report and a same-week alert on config drift. Add-on: a field check that cameras a council ordered off are really off, since Evanston found them reinstalled.
why_now: 53 cities across 20 states had cancelled or rejected Flock by mid-2026 over unauthorized federal access. New state laws (Colorado SB 26-070 warrant rule, Washington SB 6002, Kentucky HB 58 90-day retention cap, Maine's ALPR law) add compliance duties. Atlanta's ordinance, held in committee and taken up again in September 2026, would require monthly internal access audits and annual independent technical audits managed by the City Auditor. Drone-as-first-responder approvals (Stockton, Federal Way, Santa Fe, Whittier) are expanding the audit surface.
revenue_model: $4.5k one-time baseline configuration and log audit, then $1.2k-2.5k/month monitoring and quarterly council report. Upsell: annual independent technical audit that ordinances like Atlanta's require, priced $15k-40k for larger cities. Multi-year contracts through city auditor offices.
non_obvious_insight: The market is created by oversight ordinances, not by the surveillance vendors. Every ordinance that says 'audit monthly' is an unfunded mandate on a three-person auditor's office, and the failure mode is configuration drift, not sophisticated data science. Evidence: Mountain View's statewide lookup ran from launch until Jan 5, 2026 unnoticed (https://www.mv-voice.com/police/2026/01/30/amid-immigration-crackdown-mountain-view-discovers-unauthorized-access-to-license-plate-data/). The audit findings and 53-city cancellation count are in https://www.techtimes.com/articles/319317/20260629/flock-safety-crosses-100000-cameras-53-cities-cancel-over-unauthorized-federal-data-access.htm. Atlanta's proposed monthly internal and annual independent audits are at https://www.atlantanewsfirst.com/2026/09/22/atlanta-weighs-sweeping-rules-monthly-audits-surveillance-tech/. New Hanover County's commissioners called for 'explicit guardrails' before restoring cameras: https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9840468/north-carolina/new-hanover-county/commissioners-cite-privacy-shifting-vendor-policies-and-misuse-when-cancelling-flock-alpr-contract. Cities that keep the cameras need proof of compliance to survive the next council vote, and the audit report is that proof.
first_30_days: File public-records requests in about 25 cities that cancelled or kept ALPR for the audit-log export format and sharing-settings history, and build a parser for it. Produce one free 'configuration drift' teardown for a friendly city attorney or a councilmember who championed the cancellation. Pitch the $4.5k baseline audit to auditors and attorneys in cities with surveillance-oversight ordinances (Seattle, San Diego, Oakland, Cambridge, Urbana) and to those now drafting them (Atlanta). Sign 3 pilots. Main risk: vendor cooperation and export formats, so start with cities that already run their own audits.

title: Ceiling-Camera Auto-Logging for Strength Gyms
one_liner: Cameras that watch the lifting floor and automatically log every athlete's sets, reps, load and bar speed with no phone.
customer: Independent strength gyms, CrossFit boxes, powerlifting clubs and high school and college weight rooms paying $199-499 per month.
problem: Progress tracking is the strongest retention lever in lifting, but manual logging is tedious so most members skip it, and coaches at high athlete ratios cannot see everyone's sets or spot stalls.
solution: Two to four ceiling cameras plus an edge box; vision models recognize the exercise, plate colors (load), rep count and bar velocity; lifters are identified by wristband or QR rather than faces; a coach dashboard flags stalls, form drift and missed sessions and a member app fills logs automatically.
why_now: 2025-26 vision foundation models handle exercise and object recognition at the edge on cheap hardware, and tightening biometric privacy laws push products toward non-facial identification.
revenue_model: $199-499 per gym per month plus $1.5-3k install; school weight-room licenses; velocity-based-training analytics as an add-on.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the coach or owner, not the member: automatic logging gives coaches visibility that drives retention and coaching upsells, a Hudl for the weight room. Avoiding face recognition sidesteps biometric-law exposure.
first_30_days: Install DIY hardware (about $800) in two friendly gyms, label two weeks of squat, bench and deadlift footage with plate detection, offer a free three-month pilot, and measure log completion and member retention to justify $299 per month.

title: Pharma Load Attribution for EU Producer-Pays Wastewater
one_liner: A neutral, audit-grade dataset showing which drugs from which producers, in which aging catchments and care homes, create the micropollutant load that EU pharma companies must now pay at least 80% of treatment for.
customer: National extended-producer-responsibility scheme operators and pharma/cosmetics trade bodies. Regional water boards and utilities deciding which large plants get quaternary treatment first also buy. Pricing is EUR 25-80k per study and EUR 100-250k a year for licenses.
problem: The recast Urban Wastewater Directive makes pharma and cosmetics producers fund at least 80% of quaternary treatment. The payment scheme is due by end-2028, and 20% of large plants must be upgraded by 2033. Annual cost estimates differ about 10x (EC EUR 1.2B, JRC EUR 1.56B, EurEau EUR 3.6-11.2B, Spain alone EUR 24.5B), and nobody owns the attribution of kilograms of active ingredient to payers. Older adults, care homes and hospitals are the concentrated source of medication residues, and Europe's 80+ cohort is its fastest-growing.
solution: A catchment-level model combining national dispensing statistics by age band, care-home and hospital bed registers, excretion and plant-removal rates, and receiving-water flow. It is validated by composite sampling at a handful of plants. It outputs load by active ingredient by plant, mapped to marketing-authorization-holder market shares for an allocation formula. A 'source-control screen' flags plants where pretreatment at a large care home or hospital removes more load per euro than plant-scale ozone or activated carbon, as a candidate for levy credits. The methodology is published so the scheme operator can defend it.
why_now: The directive is in transposition and the scheme design is being fought over now. The 10x cost disagreement means both utilities and producers need defensible numbers before 2028. European aging keeps raising per-capita medication load.
revenue_model: Per-study fees of EUR 25-80k for water boards. Annual licenses of EUR 100-250k to national scheme operators and industry associations for the allocation engine and yearly re-runs. Later, consulting on care-home source-control projects.
non_obvious_insight: The cost fight will be won by whoever supplies a referee-grade attribution dataset. The best predictor of load is not at the pipe but at the pillbox: age-structured dispensing and care-home density explain most of it. Demographics is the missing variable in water-quality economics, and neither water engineers nor pharma-market analysts hold both halves.
first_30_days: Start with the Netherlands and Germany, where open national dispensing statistics exist (for example the Dutch GIP databank). Model 5 mid-size catchments. Cold-pitch two regional water boards and one pharma producer association with the one-page result. Aim to close paid pilots at EUR 15-25k.

title: IEP Chief of Staff for Special-Ed Parents
one_liner: Rich parents win school disputes with a paid educational advocate and paper trail; for $20/mo, give parents of the roughly 7.5M US students with IEPs a chief of staff who watches the legal clocks and logs every missed service minute.
customer: Parents of children with IEPs (autism, ADHD, dyslexia, speech and language delay), sold through state and local special-ed parent groups, parent training centers, pediatric practices, disability law clinics and credit unions.
problem: Districts arrive with a team; wealthy families bring an advocate ($150-400/hr) and an attorney. Federal enforcement was hollowed out (mass OSEP layoffs in October 2025, and reported moves of oversight to HHS and civil-rights enforcement to DOJ in June 2026), so parents are effectively on their own. Most violations are procedural (late evaluations, missing prior written notice, services not delivered) and go unnoticed because nobody keeps the clocks.
solution: Parent uploads the IEP and evaluations. The system builds the legal calendar (evaluation timelines from consent, meeting-notice windows, annual and triennial reviews, progress-report cadence), drafts records requests, creates a one-page pre-meeting brief (top asks plus data), and sends a same-day 'memorializing' follow-up email with prior-written-notice requests after meetings. It logs service minutes delivered vs promised, quantifying missed minutes for a compensatory-services claim, and scans the IEP for defects (no baselines, unmeasurable goals). Advocates are on-demand at $75 per 30 minutes, with a path to state complaint and due process.
why_now: The federal special-ed enforcement vacuum is documented and new as of late 2025 and mid-2026. IEP counts are rising, and LLMs can parse messy IEP PDFs and draft procedurally precise letters. Parent communities are organized on Facebook and Reddit and actively looking for help.
revenue_model: $20/mo per family; $75 advocate sessions with a revenue split to a vetted advocate co-op; $3-6 per member per month from parent centers, pediatric groups and credit unions; district-facing analytics sold only with parent consent, later.
non_obvious_insight: What the rich buy is not better argument but continuous procedural pressure: dated, written, specific requests. The subscription funds clock-watching and documentation, not advice. Parents who log service minutes turn 'I feel they're not delivering' into a quantified claim, and the paper trail is the evidence in any later dispute, so value compounds over time.
first_30_days: Publish a free IEP clock calculator and letter templates. Partner with admins of 10 state-level special-ed Facebook groups and concierge 30 families manually, measuring violations found. Convert those families to $20/mo and recruit 5 advocates for the on-demand tier.

title: Pre-Inspected Wildfire Books From Moratorium Zip Codes
one_liner: Turn California's public nonrenewal-moratorium ZIP lists into a supply of mitigation-verified risks, sold to carriers and MGAs who want good business and to commercial-residential owners who need it.
customer: Two payers. Admitted and E&S carriers or MGAs pay $75-150 per bound policy for a pre-inspected, standardized risk file. HOAs, apartment owners, senior-living operators and nonprofits pay $300-1,500 per building for verified defensible-space and hardening reports.
problem: California's wildfire nonrenewal moratoria last one year from the emergency declaration (up to 24 months for total losses), then the protection ends. More than 147,000 policyholders sit in 29 Gifford Fire ZIP codes, and over 64,000 in 22 Gann Fire ZIP codes. Since SB 547 took effect on 2026-01-01, commercial residential owners are covered for the first time, so they will face renewal shock too. Carriers lack standardized ground-truth mitigation evidence, and owners have no cheap way to produce it.
solution: A mitigation-verification package aligned to the state's Safer from Wildfires discount framework. It covers ember-resistant vents, Zone 0 clearance, roof class, and geotagged photo evidence with an inspector attestation. The result is a portable underwriting file. We start with commercial residential buildings, where one manager decision covers many units and the owners are reachable, and then sell the file to carriers as a pre-underwritten book.
why_now: The Gifford Fire moratorium (emergency declared 2025-12-23) expires around 2026-12-23, about 86 days from today. The Gann Fire moratorium began 2026-08-06. The FAIR Plan hit 696,562 policies and $768B of exposure in June 2026, up 157% and 250% since September 2022. Carriers have been restricting writing statewide, and the state has told them to give wildfire safety discounts.
revenue_model: Inspection fees from commercial-residential owners ($300-1,500 per building), plus per-bind fees or a basis-point share of premium from carriers and MGAs taking the verified files. Later upsell of reinspection subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: The moratorium notices are effectively a public, geocoded list of about 210,000 policyholders whose insurability will be decided by mitigation evidence within months. See https://www.insurance.ca.gov/0400-news/0100-press-releases/2025/release002-2026.cfm (Gifford: 147,000+ policyholders, 29 ZIPs, one year from 2025-12-23, up to 24 months for total loss, SB 547 extends to businesses, associations, affordable housing, senior facilities and nonprofits) and https://www.insurance.ca.gov/0400-news/0100-press-releases/2026/release027-2026.cfm (Gann: 64,000+, 22 ZIPs). FAIR Plan growth is at https://www.cfpnet.com/key-statistics-data/. Cotality found 2.5M US properties with $1.4T wildfire exposure (https://www.cotality.com/press-releases/over-2-5m-u-s-properties-face-wildfire-risk-with-1-4tn-exposed). I could not confirm carrier re-entry commitments in this session, so the carrier-side demand is a hypothesis to test with 3 MGAs before scaling. The wedge sells to reachable commercial-residential owners first, and the carrier data sale follows once the files exist.
first_30_days: Download the ZIP lists for Gifford and Gann and geocode commercial-residential buildings (HOAs, apartments, senior living) from county parcel and permit data. Train 2 inspectors on a one-page checklist based on the state discount framework. Cold-call 40 property managers in the Gifford ZIPs before 2026-12-23 and offer a discounted first inspection. Show 3 MGAs sample files and ask what fields they would pay for.

title: Add Megawatt-Hours to Already-Interconnected Batteries
one_liner: The queue limits megawatts, not megawatt-hours, so sell cheap add-on energy blocks to existing 2-hour battery and solar sites that already own the grid connection.
customer: Owners of 2019-2024 vintage 2-hour storage and solar sites (IPPs, infrastructure funds, utilities) in PJM, ERCOT and CAISO. Storage developers and data center developers who lack queue positions are the second buyer group.
problem: New MW wait years in interconnection queues. Stationary packs fell 45% to about $70/kWh and new projects average 3.5 hours. Existing 2-hour fleets are under-accredited for capacity, and their owners are not thinking about bolt-on energy.
solution: Engineer and finance duration uplift by adding DC-coupled or AC-block MWh behind the existing inverters and point of interconnection. Provide standardized BMS integration and warranty tooling. Second product: use surplus interconnection headroom at solar and wind farms to add storage MW, with a revenue share to the site owner. The company screens sites from public data, packages them and sells them or builds them.
why_now: Cell prices collapsed. Capacity prices at the cap reward accredited duration. Regulators (surplus interconnection service, MISO ERAS, PJM RRI) are openly trying to reuse existing grid connections.
revenue_model: Engineering and development fee per kWh added, a share of incremental capacity revenue, or resale of ready-to-build projects.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is the interconnection agreement, not the battery. Every existing 2-hour battery is a queue position with half its energy potential unused, and it is the one capacity addition that skips the queue.
first_30_days: List ~200 US storage projects at 2 hours or less from EIA-860 and ISO data. Model uplift economics for 10 of them under PJM and ERCOT rules. Send owners a one-page 'what two more hours earns you' analysis. Sign two or three paid feasibility studies. Line up a non-FEOC DC block supplier.

title: Vacancy-Permit Kit for Half-Empty Offices
one_liner: A sensor and inspection package that keeps half-empty office buildings insurable and safe during the 12-36 months of limbo before resolution.
customer: Special servicers, receivers and owners of office buildings under roughly 31% occupancy or with dark floors, plus lender-placed insurance managers.
problem: Many standard commercial property forms treat a building as vacant unless about 31% of its area is leased and in use, and after 60 days of vacancy exclude vandalism, water damage, theft and glass while cutting other payouts (buildings under renovation are exempt). Meanwhile stagnant plumbing raises Legionella risk, HVAC is wasted, and squatters and fire watch add cost. About 15.7% of office CMBS is in special servicing, and resolutions take years.
solution: Flow and temperature sensors with automated flush valves, HVAC setback tied to the building system, AI door and intrusion cameras and documented monthly inspections. Packaged as evidence for a vacancy permit or protective-safeguards endorsement and as reporting to servicers, installed only on dark floors.
why_now: Distress is at record levels with long resolutions, property insurance is costly and restrictive, and IoT and video analytics are cheap.
revenue_model: $0.10-0.30 per sf per year subscription plus $1-3 per sf install, with referral fees from commercial insurance brokers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is writing about conversion, but nobody services the limbo period where value leaks through insurance denials and stagnant water. A few dollars of sensors can be cheaper than one uninsured water loss.
first_30_days: Partner with two commercial brokers who place vacant-building coverage. Pilot at two receiver-owned buildings for about $5K each. Ask an insurer to accept the protocol in writing.

title: GLP-1 Size-Curve Index for Apparel Planners
one_liner: A monthly 'size-shift index' that tells merchandise planners, airlines and furniture makers how GLP-1 adoption is moving their customers' bodies.
customer: Merchandise planners and size-curve analysts at apparel, footwear and outdoor brands and off-price retailers, plus airline, cruise, furniture and medical-equipment planners.
problem: Households with a GLP-1 user doubled to ~22%, and users lose double-digit percentages of body weight in a year. Retailers still plan size curves on last year's sell-through, which lags, causing markdowns on the wrong sizes. CFOs are already modeling downstream effects (Jefferies estimates ~$600M/yr airline fuel savings).
solution: Build an index by region, age and gender from licensed or partner data (pharmacy-fill proxies where affordable, retailer size and returns data, sizing surveys, public health data) and forecast size-curve migration by category. Deliver an API, a quarterly briefing, and a custom-model add-on.
why_now: Adoption accelerated after the 2026 pill launches. BCG and GoodRx data show measurable spend shifts (less pasta and bakery, more fragrance, skincare and supplements), so consumer-goods planners are hunting for leading indicators.
revenue_model: $40-120k/year per retailer or brand, plus $20-60k custom-modeling projects.
non_obvious_insight: Sell-through is a lagging indicator, and the drug adoption curve by ZIP is a leading one. It is a healthcare-adjacent data business with no clinical regulation if built on aggregated data, so a two-person team can sell it to non-healthcare budgets.
first_30_days: Build v0 from public data (NHANES, BRFSS, Google Trends) plus a 2,000-person sizing survey. Email 30 planners with a free size-shift report for one category and offer partner-data-in-exchange pricing. Sign one $15k pilot.

title: Robot-Training Disassembly Lab for E-Scrap Magnets
one_liner: A small teardown shop where displaced office workers are paid to take apart hard drives and servers on camera, so sales of robot-training data cover the labor that makes rare-earth magnet recovery uneconomic.
customer: Two paying buyers. (1) Physical-AI and robotics labs that need real contact-rich manipulation data. (2) Rare-earth processors and ITAD firms that want magnets and boards already pulled out of steel and PCB streams. The workers are laid-off office staff and underemployed recent grads.
problem: The circular-materials brief says the rare-earth bottleneck is collection and disassembly, not chemistry, and that pulling magnets from hard drives often costs more than the magnets are worth. Robotics labs are short of messy, real-world demonstration data. Meanwhile the expert-gig data economy (Mercor and similar) pays only for screen work, contractors complain of falling pay, and recent-grad underemployment is 42%.
solution: Rent a bay near an ITAD or data-center decommissioner and take in drives and servers that are already sanitized under NIST 800-88. Workers wear head cameras and instrumented gloves or tool sensors and follow step protocols. An annotation pipeline labels screw types, connectors and failure cases. Sell the licensed video and force data by the annotated hour. Sell the pre-extracted magnet fractions, aluminum and boards to processors. Later, the same corpus trains a disassembly arm that lowers labor cost. Workers earn wages plus a skills log.
why_now: Physical-AI funding and data hunger are at a peak in 2026. DoD and DOE are subsidizing domestic rare-earth supply, and hyperscalers are pushing processors to recover magnets. DRAM prices are up about 400% since early 2024, and data centers turn hardware over every 12-18 months, so teardown yield keeps rising. White-collar hiring is frozen for the young (Stanford: 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs are 19% below trend).
revenue_model: Data licensing per annotated hour (hypothesis to test: $35-60/hr, versus roughly $25-28/hr loaded labor). Materials sales of magnets, aluminum, boards and DRAM/SSD. Per-unit processing fees from ITAD partners. Later, licensing the teardown protocols and a robot-ready dataset.
non_obvious_insight: Disassembly looks unprofitable only because we value just the recovered material. The task has a second output, training data, that has no recovery-cost floor. The uglier and more variable the end-of-life product, the more out-of-distribution and valuable the data is to robotics labs. Recycling's mess is the data moat, and the displaced labor is the cheap input.
first_30_days: Sign one ITAD or decommissioner for a free lot of about 500 sanitized drives. Sign one robotics team for a paid 100-hour pilot. Recruit six workers from laid-off tech and helpdesk groups. Build three capture stations (camera plus glove rig, about $1.5K each). Sell the first magnet and aluminum lot to a local processor to prove the unit economics.

title: Steeple Sites: Church Land for Satellite Ground Stations
one_liner: Master-lease deals with denominations to host satellite ground stations, gateways and RF sensors on steeples and surplus church land, sold to operators as a ready-made site portfolio.
customer: Ground-station-as-a-service networks, smallsat IoT and EO operators, and direct-to-cell or broadband constellation operators needing gateways. Congregations and dioceses are paid as hosts.
problem: Launch has flooded orbit (321 launches, 4,517 satellites deployed in 2025, about 10,400 Starlinks), and carrier partnerships are multiplying, so downlink capacity, gateways and RF-quiet sites are a constraint. Site acquisition is slow, one farm or roof at a time. Meanwhile congregations own tall, zoning-friendly structures and acreage, monthly attendance is stuck at about 33%, and many boards need rental income or surplus-property solutions.
solution: Negotiate master-lease templates with denominational property boards (diocesan or conference trustees). Pre-screen sites for line of sight, RF noise, power, fiber and zoning, and package them into portfolios by latitude and orbit. Partner integrators handle permitting and install, and congregations get a share.
why_now: The spectrum land-grab settled (EchoStar's $23B sale to AT&T closed in July 2026, and the $17B sale to SpaceX), MNO satellite deals are multiplying, and every country-level service needs terrestrial infrastructure. Congregation attendance has plateaued at a low level, so property decisions are live.
revenue_model: A $5-15k site-acquisition fee per signed site paid by the operator, 15-20% of lease revenue for the life of the lease, and install margin. Congregations target $6-24k per year (to be validated).
non_obvious_insight: The tower industry already proved steeples are leasable, tall, permitted and governed by a few trustees, but satellite site teams chase farmland. One denomination negotiation can unlock hundreds of sites, and a closing parish is a seller with time pressure.
first_30_days: Pick one diocese or conference with rural clusters and pitch a pro-bono pilot lease template. Screen 30 sites from imagery, and approach 3 ground-network or IoT operators with a shortlist for a country where they lack coverage. Charge a $2-5k site-survey fee for a 10-site report as the first revenue.

title: Low-Background Human Data: Witnessed Creative Corpora
one_liner: Like pre-war steel, certifiably human creative work is becoming scarce, so sell fresh, witnessed, process-verified corpora to labs and detector vendors.
customer: AI labs and evaluation teams, detector vendors that need gold human test sets, and data-licensing brokers.
problem: Anything scraped from the web after 2023 is contaminated (AI is over 50% of Deezer daily uploads, and large shares of text are machine-made). Labs need uncontaminated creative data for evals, style diversity and fine-tuning. Detector vendors need known-human sets to measure false positives. No one can currently prove any given item is human.
solution: A paid panel of ID-verified writers, illustrators and musicians produce work under witnessed capture (screen and keystroke logs, DAW session logs, timelapse). Each item ships with process evidence in a quarterly dataset subscription. Creators are paid per item plus royalties from dataset revenue. Start with a 5,000-item 'human baseline' across text, illustration and music.
why_now: Contamination is now measurable, detector-scoring consequences are public, and human data has become a large market. Process-capture tooling for creative apps is cheap.
revenue_model: $25-300k per dataset subscription, per-item pricing of $5-200, and evaluation-as-a-service, with 50-60% of revenue to creators.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce good is not more data but certifiably unpolluted data, and every improvement in AI raises its price. The premium for 'guaranteed human' is set by buyers who cannot get it anywhere else.
first_30_days: Recruit 100 creators from paid-newsletter and Discord communities. Build a capture app (browser extension plus DAW logging). Send a sample data card to detector vendors and two labs' eval teams, and sell a $25-75k baseline set.

title: Mindbody Escape Hatch: Studio Migration Concierge
one_liner: A flat-fee service that moves a studio's members, class packs and payment tokens off Mindbody without losing revenue.
customer: Boutique studios, gyms, yoga and Pilates operators on Mindbody (about 40,000 businesses) paying $159-699 per month plus marketplace commissions.
problem: After the ClassPass/Mindbody/EGYM combination (a $7.5B deal completed in 2026), owners report about 23.5 percent effective marketplace commissions and a roughly $500 data-export fee on cancellation. Lock-in is not the software but the card-on-file payment tokens and member history, so owners fear migration will churn members.
solution: A fixed-fee migration ($1.5-3k): export clients, attendance, waivers, packs and memberships; execute PCI-compliant processor-to-processor token migration; map intro offers and unlimited plans; rebuild schedule widgets; run parallel billing checks; and message members by SMS. Target alternative platforms pay a bounty per migrated studio.
why_now: Consolidation gave studios a reason to re-evaluate, ClassPass is rolling out studio-friendly policies in response to complaints, and processors now support token migration.
revenue_model: $1.5-3k per migration plus $200-400 bounty per studio from the receiving software vendor and an optional $99 per month retention audit.
non_obvious_insight: The moat is edge-case knowledge (paused members, unlimited plans, refunds, tokens), not software, and rival vendors will pay you for customers because their own acquisition cost is high.
first_30_days: Offer five free migration audits in studio-owner communities, pick two target platforms, run three at-cost pilot migrations, and turn the playbook into a checklist and pricing page.

title: Bot-Proof Local Comments: Verified Neighbors, Pseudonymous
one_liner: Secret and Yik Yak died of unaccountable anonymity and Digg's March 2026 relaunch died of bots; the missing primitive is 'one real human, from this place, no real name', and local newsrooms and city councils will pay for it.
customer: Independent and nonprofit local newsrooms (hundreds exist) that have switched off comments, and city, county and school-board clerks running public comment for hearings on rezonings, data centers and levies.
problem: Newsrooms disabled comment sections because of toxicity and bots, so local conversation moved to Facebook groups. Public bodies get astroturf and AI-generated comment floods (the 2017 FCC net-neutrality docket was later found mostly fake by New York's attorney general) and cannot tell residents from out-of-area campaigns or bots.
solution: An embeddable comment and public-comment widget. Each person verifies once via a state mobile ID in Apple or Google Wallet with address check, or a postcard PIN or voter-file match as fallback, then posts under a pseudonym. The platform attests only 'verified human, resident of ZIP or ward X'. Public bodies get a verified-resident tally (for example, '412 verified residents commented, 78% opposed, 61 from Ward 3'). One credential works across the paper, council and school board, and publishers never see identity.
why_now: Digg's open beta launched 14 January 2026 and shut on 14 March 2026 after bot and AI-agent floods. Agents can now write plausible public comments at scale. Mobile IDs in phone wallets make cheap, high-assurance verification possible. Local news funders are paying for audience-trust infrastructure.
revenue_model: $200-1,500/mo per newsroom; $500-3,000/mo per municipality or agency for a verified public-comment portal; per-verification fees ($0.50-1.50) sponsored by foundations or civic funders; later, verified local polling panels.
non_obvious_insight: Anonymity was never the fatal flaw; unverifiable anonymity was. In a bot-saturated internet, 'provably a real neighbor' becomes the scarce good, and local institutions already need it but cannot buy it. The credential also compounds: a resident verified once for the newspaper is reusable for council, school board and library levy comments.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 small newsrooms through nonprofit-news networks to run a verified-comment pilot on one hot local issue (rezoning or data center) using SMS or postcard plus voter-file match. Publish the verified-tally story, then pitch the same town's clerk a public-comment pilot. Charge $250/mo after the pilot.

title: Managed Migrations When Models Get Retired
one_liner: We replay your agent's real traces on the replacement model, fix the regressions, and hand back a patched prompt and tool config with a pass/fail report before the deprecation date.
customer: Series A-C SaaS companies and enterprise automation teams running 1-20 production agents without a dedicated eval or ML team.
problem: Model versions are retired on schedules set by others (for example GitHub scheduled the removal of several Claude and Gemini versions in Copilot on 2026-09-01). When an agent is repointed to a newer model it keeps returning success codes while tool-call formatting, JSON adherence, refusal boundaries and token use silently change. Teams without eval infrastructure find out from customers.
solution: Fixed-fee migration sprints: capture golden traces, build assertions from tool traces, schemas and business rules, run baseline versus candidate models, tune prompts and tool descriptions, and report accuracy, latency and cost. A subscription Sunset Watch tracks about 20 providers' deprecation calendars and opens migration tickets automatically, with a self-serve replay tool later.
why_now: Retirement cadence accelerated across 2025-26, agents with multi-step tool use are more fragile than chat apps, and falling token prices tempt teams to switch models constantly.
revenue_model: $8-$25k per migration sprint and $1-3k/month for Sunset Watch.
non_obvious_insight: The customers who most need migration cannot afford an eval team, which is why Y2K, Java and Windows migrations became services businesses. Deprecation calendars are set by providers, so demand is scheduled and forecastable.
first_30_days: Publish a public deprecation calendar and migration-risk checklist. Cold-offer sprints to 30 companies visibly on soon-to-be-retired models (found via job posts and public integrations). Do 2 discounted pilots.

title: Cask Audit: Proof of Existence for Whisky Investors
one_liner: An independent inspection, gauging and valuation service that verifies investor-owned whisky casks exist, contain what was sold, and are worth what the seller says.
customer: Retail cask investors, IFAs and wealth managers, insolvency practitioners and law firms, and honest cask brokers who want a trust seal.
problem: The cask market has been in a glut since 2022 (auction surplus, distillery consolidation, lower price per litre) and has documented fraud cases where audits found casks missing or filled with substandard spirit. Investors cannot verify holdings or exit.
solution: Field inspectors in bonded warehouses attest existence, fill level, strength, cask type and warehouse-receipt ownership, with geotagged photos. Quarterly valuations use bottling yield and market comps, and brokers pay to join an 'audited cask' registry.
why_now: In a downturn demand shifts from buying more to proving what you own. Fraud taints every honest broker, so third-party proof is worth paying for.
revenue_model: GBP 150-300 per cask audit, broker subscriptions for continuous audit, and valuation reports.
non_obvious_insight: Bonded-warehouse access is already a contractual owner right, so inspectors are cheap to deploy, while buyers of proof are motivated by loss and by seller reputation. The bourbon cask market is a later expansion. Confirm warehouse cooperation and local regulation early.
first_30_days: Recruit 2 warehouse-keepers, audit 30 casks for 10 investors at a GBP 100 pilot rate, publish anonymized findings, and approach IFAs and insolvency firms.

title: Screw-Pile Foundations That Skip the Concrete Crew
one_liner: Engineered helical-pile foundations with torque-logged QA and prefab floor cassettes, installed in a day, for spec homes, ADUs and factory-built homes where foundation crews are booked out for weeks.
customer: Spec and production builders in crew-constrained markets (Texas, Florida), ADU builders and factory-built home dealers.
problem: Foundations sit 30+ days waiting for crews, and loan interest keeps accruing while 15-20 houses wait 6+ weeks. Forming, pouring and finishing are crew-dependent and hard to automate. Chassis-free factory homes need light foundations that are quick to install.
solution: A foundation-only subcontractor installing helical piles with a torque-monitoring logger and structural details pre-approved by a partner engineer for three soil regions, plus a prefab insulated floor cassette or steel grade beam. Torque logs become an objective, timestamped QA report for inspectors and lenders. Autonomous pile driving, already proven in solar, is the roadmap.
why_now: Enforcement and labor shortages are stretching foundation crews. Autonomous pile-driving rigs are commercial in solar. Chassis-free homes and the ADU boom create demand for light foundations. Lenders and inspectors increasingly accept digital QA data.
revenue_model: Priced roughly at parity with slab or stem-wall per home and sold on speed, with margin from utilization. Per-sq-ft or per-home pricing, plus licensing engineered details to other installers.
non_obvious_insight: Changing the design removes the scarce trade from the critical path entirely. Insiders try to hire or automate concrete crews, but a foundation with no forms, no cure time and no finishers becomes a machine-and-engineering task with objective logs.
first_30_days: Engage a geotech and a structural PE for standard details. Rent a mini-excavator with a torque head. Sign two builders with stuck lots or ADUs, install three foundations, and document schedule savings versus their alternatives.

title: Grant Recovery Desk for Small Cities
one_liner: A contingency-fee grant compliance and reimbursement service for small cities receiving FEMA, DOJ and counter-drone money with no staff to document it.
customer: Towns and counties with populations of 5-100K, especially those receiving disaster reimbursements and new safety grants (for example the $500M FEMA counter-UAS program).
problem: Small governments lose federal reimbursements to incomplete documentation, procurement missteps and audit findings. With federal agencies shrinking and reorganizations stalled in court, help is thinner. Dallas County is cutting IT staff, and local budgets are tight.
solution: A software-plus-service program that structures the grant lifecycle: eligibility check, procurement compliance, receipt capture, quarterly reporting and closeout audit packages. It uses AI to read award terms and flag non-compliant purchases before they happen. Paid from recovered funds.
why_now: New grant streams (counter-drone, cyber, disaster) are landing at localities while federal grant-management staff are being cut. Regulators enforce documentation harder as budgets tighten.
revenue_model: Contingency of 4-8% of recovered or protected award dollars, with a minimum retainer. A city with $2M in awards yields about $80-160K.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer pays nothing up front, and the alternative is losing money already awarded. Contingency pricing turns a dreaded compliance cost into free money for a small clerk's office.
first_30_days: Offer free award-file reviews to 10 small cities identified from public award lists. Build a compliance checklist per program. Sign 2 contingency deals.
